input.question: How is it possible that everything falls at the same speed regardless of mass? Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct?
input.ground_truth: > Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct? Yes. The "limit of the approximation" is that the mass of the thing dropped is negligible compared to the mass of the Earth. Consider two masses M1 and M2 at a distance R. The gravitational force F between them will be G\*M1\*M2/R^2 , so the acceleration of the first object will be F/M1 = G\*M2/R^2 and the acceleration of the second object will be F/M2 = G\*M1/R^2 The two objects will thus accelerate towards each other at a rate of G\*(M1 + M2)/R^2 . In the case of a feather or hammer on the Earth, M1 is so much larger than M2 that the effects of M2 can be ignored. In this case, both hammer and feather would have the same acceleration.

Okay, let's imagine you have a big rock and a tiny feather. If you drop them at the same time (and there’s no wind), they both hit the ground at the same time! That seems weird because the rock is heavier, right? But here’s why:

**Imagine there’s something called “air” that pushes up a little on things. Feathers are big and light, so the air pushes them a lot and they fall slowly. But if you do this in a place with no air (like on the Moon), both the big rock and the tiny feather fall *exactly* at the same speed!**

Why? Well, the Earth pulls everything down with a force that depends on how heavy it is. But the heavy things also have more “stuff” to push through the air (or, if there’s no air, nothing to slow them down). It all balances out so that, if there’s no air, everything falls at the same speed.

But wait! This is only *almost* true on Earth because of air. In a place with no air, like the Moon, it’s *exactly* true.

Also, this rule is an *approximation*. If things are super, super fast or super, super heavy (like a spaceship or a planet), or if we get really, really close to a super strong gravity (like near a black hole), then this rule doesn’t work anymore. But for things we see every day, it works really well!

So, in simple words:  
**Everything falls at the same speed in places with no air because the Earth pulls harder on heavier things, but they also have more “stuff” to slow them down. When there’s no air, nothing slows them down, so they all fall together! And this rule is almost true here on Earth, except for things the air slows down a lot, like feathers. And it’s not exactly true for really big or fast things.**
